title: New quantum heat engine produces work and refrigeration at same time
summary: Researchers at Qufu Normal University, the University of Hong Kong and the University of Palermo built a quantum Otto engine that simultaneously produces mechanical work and refrigeration by exploiting anomalous heat flow enabled by indefinite causal order and other quantum effects. The experiment confirms theoretical predictions and opens paths for new quantum technologies that manipulate heat and energy in unconventional ways.
content:
A collaboration of researchers across international borders observed an anomalous thermal effect that allows quantum systems to absorb heat from cold thermal reservoirs. The team then leveraged this behavior to build a quantum heat engine that can produce mechanical work and refrigeration at the same time.

Classical physics tells us that heat naturally flows from systems at higher temperature to those at lower temperature. This principle has been used to develop a range of technologies from power plants to household refrigerators, and it applies until an equilibrium between the two systems has been reached.

When researchers at Qufu Normal University, the University of Hong Kong and the University of Palermo observed an anomalous thermal behavior due to quantum effects, they immediately thought of possible applications. The result was a heat engine that operates on two processes simultaneously and exploits distinctly quantum features.

"Indefinite Causal Order (ICO) allows two events to occur in a superposition of orders," explained Zhong-Xiao Man, a researcher in quantum mechanics at Qufu Normal University. "Previous work has shown that even with identical channel temperatures, the system need not equilibrate to that temperature."

This is a major deviation from classical thermodynamics, and the researchers asked what would happen to heat flow when the system and channel started at different temperatures or when there are two thermal reservoirs. In theoretical work they predicted that the quantum system could absorb heat from colder thermal reservoirs — an effect impossible in classical thermodynamics.

To test the prediction they built a quantum Otto engine that experimentally demonstrated the unusual heat flow. "In the quantum world, two thermal processes can occur in a superposition of different orders. This creates an unusual heat flow, allowing the engine to draw energy from a colder environment in a way that would not be possible classically," Man said.

By bringing a theoretical concept to physical reality, the researchers demonstrated that the effects are not just signatures of indefinite causal order but can also be reproduced with defined causal structure. That is, the anomalous thermal behavior can arise in setups where the causal sequence is well defined, broadening the contexts in which the effect may be realized.

The work is a proof of principle that may help design other quantum technologies able to manipulate heat and energy in new ways. Potential applications include quantum processors, sensors and other devices where control of energy flows at the quantum scale is important.

"One area for future research is to move beyond idealized thermodynamic cycles and investigate more realistic implementations where all operations occur in a finite time," said Rosario Lo Franco, a researcher in Open Quantum Systems at the University of Palermo who was involved in the work. "In practical devices, speed matters because it determines not only efficiency but also power output. Recent theoretical studies have shown that finite-time measurements and control operations can introduce fundamental trade-offs between energetic cost, information gain and performance, and we would like to understand how these limitations affect the type of engine proposed in our work."

The research findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters. The experiment and analysis demonstrate a route toward engines that combine work extraction and on-board refrigeration by using quantum superposition of process orders and related phenomena. Continued study will explore how these effects scale, how robust they are under realistic noise and timing constraints, and how to integrate them into functional quantum devices.

Ameya Paleja is a science writer based in Hyderabad, India. A molecular biologist by training, he now covers science topics including genetics, microbes, technology and public policy.
